key_features.classic_presentation: ONSET: GRADUAL to SUDDEN onset within 1-3 days (subacute). Not as dramatic as appendicitis. LOCATION: LEFT LOWER QUADRANT (LLQ) - key differentiator from appendicitis (RLQ). LOCALIZED and CONSTANT. Sometimes palpable tender mass. DURATION: CONSTANT pain lasting hours to days (not episodic). Persists continuously. CHARACTER: ACHING or SHARP, CONSTANT pain. Steady, unrelenting quality. AGGRAVATING: MOVEMENT worsens pain. Bowel movements may increase discomfort. RELIEVING: Rest and lying still provide slight relief. NOTHING fully relieves. Antibiotics needed for resolution. TIMING: CONSTANT throughout. May worsen progressively. Not wave-like or crampy. SEVERITY: 6-9/10, moderate to severe. ASSOCIATED SYMPTOMS: LOW-GRADE FEVER (100-101°F), change in bowel habits (DIARRHEA or constipation), nausea, anorexia. KEY POSITIVES: LLQ tenderness, fever, age >40, known diverticulosis, low-fiber diet history. KEY NEGATIVES: RIGHT-sided pain suggests appendicitis. HIGH FEVER >102°F suggests abscess/perforation. PROFUSE diarrhea suggests gastroenteritis. Age <40 makes unlikely.

red_flags: Severe LLQ pain with high fever >102°F and rigors - diverticular abscess, needs CT and possible drainage
Sudden severe pain with peritoneal signs - perforation with peritonitis, call 911
Unable to tolerate oral intake with vomiting - possible obstruction from inflammation
Immunocompromised patients - higher risk of perforation and sepsis
